questions.question: What is the main purpose of the long parallel mid-body on a bulk carrier?
questions.explanation: The long parallel mid-body provides maximum internal volume for cargo holds, increasing cargo capacity.

questions.question: What is the typical block coefficient (Cb) of a bulk carrier?
questions.explanation: Bulk carriers have a full-form hull with a block coefficient typically between 0.70 and 0.80.

questions.question: Why do bulk carriers usually have a high ballast capacity?
options: To maintain an efficient draft and propeller immersion when unloaded
To reduce the size of the cargo holds
questions.explanation: Large ballast tanks help maintain proper draft, trim and propeller immersion during ballast voyages.

questions.question: Which stern design is commonly used on modern bulk carriers?
questions.explanation: Modern bulk carriers almost universally use a transom stern for improved hydrodynamic performance.

questions.question: Why are bulk carrier hulls longitudinally stiffened?
questions.explanation: Bulk carriers experience significant longitudinal bending loads, making longitudinal stiffening the preferred structural arrangement.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of a duct keel in a double-bottom bulk carrier?
options: To provide space for pipelines and support loads during dry docking
questions.explanation: The duct keel carries pipelines and also transfers loads to keel blocks when the vessel is dry docked.

questions.question: What is the purpose of hopper tanks in bulk carrier cargo holds?
options: To improve cargo trimming and reduce cargo shifting
questions.explanation: Hopper tanks create sloped sides that help cargo flow toward the centerline, making the holds self-trimming.

questions.question: Why is the sheer strake normally thicker than the adjacent deck or side shell plating?
options: Because this area experiences high stress concentrations
questions.explanation: The deck-to-side shell connection experiences high stresses, requiring increased plate thickness.

questions.question: What is one major advantage of a double-hull bulk carrier compared to a single-hull design?
options: Improved stability and additional ballast capacity
questions.explanation: Double-hull designs provide wing ballast tanks that improve stability and increase safety.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of corrugated transverse bulkheads?
options: To eliminate the need for separate stiffeners
questions.explanation: Corrugations provide structural strength without requiring additional stiffeners, resulting in a better strength-to-weight ratio.

questions.question: What is the primary advantage of alternate hold loading?
options: It improves cargo weight distribution and minimizes cargo shifting
questions.explanation: Alternate hold loading distributes heavy cargo more evenly and keeps holds either full or empty, reducing cargo movement.

questions.question: Why are bulk carrier hatch openings made very large?
options: To allow rapid loading and unloading of bulk cargo
questions.explanation: Large hatch openings allow efficient loading and discharge using grabs, conveyors and shore equipment.

questions.question: A bulk carrier is loaded with a very dense cargo such as iron ore. Why may the loading plan require some cargo holds to remain empty?
options: To reduce longitudinal bending moments and hull stresses
questions.explanation: Very dense cargo can produce excessive bending moments if every hold is filled. Loading manuals specify allowable loading patterns.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of top-side ballast tanks on many bulk carriers?
options: To improve transverse strength and provide ballast capacity
questions.explanation: Top-side tanks contribute to hull strength while also providing ballast capacity and reducing free cargo surface.

questions.question: Why are hatch covers on bulk carriers designed to withstand very high loads?
options: Because they are part of the vessel's longitudinal strength and must withstand green seas
Because they support the accommodation block
Because ballast tanks are located inside them
Because they carry the ship's propeller shaft
questions.explanation: Hatch covers contribute to hull girder integrity and must resist sea loads, cargo loads and weather conditions.

questions.question: Why are stress concentrations around hatch corners carefully reinforced?
options: To reduce the risk of fatigue cracks developing during service
questions.explanation: Large hatch openings interrupt deck continuity and create stress concentrations that can initiate fatigue cracks.

questions.question: A bulk carrier experiences excessive sagging during loading. What does this indicate?
options: The middle part of the vessel is bending downward relative to the ends
The bow is trimming excessively by the head
The stern has lost buoyancy due to flooding
The vessel has excessive transverse list
questions.explanation: Sagging occurs when buoyancy is greater near the ends than in the middle, causing the hull girder to bend downward amidships.

questions.question: Why is a loading computer considered an essential tool on modern bulk carriers?
options: It continuously verifies stability, shear forces and bending moments during cargo operations
It automatically controls the main engine
It replaces the need for cargo planning
It determines fuel consumption based only on weather forecasts
questions.explanation: Loading computers calculate stability, trim, shear forces and bending moments to ensure the vessel remains within allowable limits.

questions.question: A survey finds corrosion in the lower stool of a cargo hold. Why is this area particularly important?
options: It transfers structural loads between the hopper tank and transverse bulkhead
It supports the main engine foundation
It carries electrical cables to the bridge
questions.explanation: Lower stools are major structural members that transfer cargo and hull loads through the bulkhead structure.

questions.question: Why can repeated loading and unloading cycles eventually lead to structural fatigue in a bulk carrier?
options: Repeated cyclic stresses gradually initiate and propagate cracks even below the material's ultimate strength
Cargo permanently increases the hull's weight after each voyage
Steel becomes softer every time ballast water is changed
The propeller produces permanent bending in the stern structure
questions.explanation: Fatigue damage develops from repeated stress cycles over many years, making inspections of critical structural areas essential.
